rationale: A small active-inference simulation can be built so that cells sharing one target morphology settle into that arrangement, and this paper's eight-cell head–body–tail runs are presented as exactly that demonstration. The result is a proof of principle inside the model, not evidence that real embryos self-assemble this way.

Casting a genome as parameters of a generative model is a coherent analogy under the free-energy framing, since DNA does set the cell's repertoire of sensors and responses. Identifying signalling-dependent transcription with inversion of a model of the target morphology is not how genetic and epigenetic control of patterning is known to work.

Cells clearly use local cues and encoded positional information, but morphogenesis does not require each cell to carry an implicit model of the whole final body and to move by sampling the signals that model predicts. Gradient, contact, and gene-regulatory mechanisms produce organized form without that active-inference requirement.

Their shared generative model can be constructed so that a unique assignment of cells to places is the free-energy minimum. Free-energy minimization does not in general guarantee arrival at that global minimum, because the same variational objective can have local minima and path dependence.

In this sort of ensemble simulation, identical agents can break symmetry by coupling each cell's fate to the signals produced by the others, then differentiate once positions stabilize. The reported migration-then-differentiation trajectory is a plausible and specific output of the model they describe.

If every cell carries the same target model, duplicating the cells of each half and letting inference continue is expected to rebuild the full pattern in silico. That is a property of the simulation, analogous to regulative embryos, not a demonstration of planarian regeneration.

Changing how strongly simulated cells weight particular signals, while leaving the generative model fixed, will distort the pattern in signal-specific ways, including a smaller head territory or failed rearrangement. Those runs are reasonable in-model predictions; they are not thereby shown to forecast real pharmacological birth defects.

Non-neural cells use gap junctions and many of the same ion-channel classes as neurons while they pattern and repair tissue, so shared dynamical motifs are a real possibility. Whether those networks are similar enough for tools built for neural circuits to transfer to morphogenesis data remains open, which the hedged claim allows.

An external gradient is a standard way to pin orientation and reduce symmetry-breaking failures as the number of identical agents grows, so a robustness gain above a handful of cells is expected in this simulation. The claim does not say the gradient is required, which matches how such models behave.

A brief bioelectric or gap-junction perturbation can durably reset planarian regenerative anatomy, including a stable two-headed pattern, so non-genetic physiological state matters for the target morphology. Equating those epigenetic processes with active inference, and calling that inference indispensable for patterning, goes beyond the evidence.

Transient octanol after decapitation does alter head shape in wild-type Girardia dorotocephala, and the regenerated outlines were reported to fall nearer the shapes of other planarian species. Octanol is not a pure gap-junction reagent, and the species match rests on one study's morphometrics rather than a broadly replicated species transformation.

Landmark-based Procrustes analysis can show that experimenter-grouped regenerates sit closer to the species whose outline they were judged to resemble than to untreated Girardia. That comparison is only partly independent of the original visual grouping, so it supports a shape shift more than a clean cross-species identity.

The same octanol treatment yielding several discrete head shapes at unequal rates fits a stochastic patterning outcome. A rank correlation with evolutionary distance is only weakly constrained by three comparison species, even if the rarer shape is the more distant polycelid.

If the whole anterior pattern is shifted, brain proportions stained for synapsin would be expected to covary with external head shape, and a significant length-to-width difference was reported. The species-level resemblance of internal brain anatomy is still a single-study morphometric claim.

Mitotic neoblasts are patterned along the planarian axis, so a changed anterior morphology can come with a changed phospho-histone distribution. That the same gap-junction-sensitive process specifically organizes stem-cell spacing in a species-typical way is an inference beyond the staining correlation.

Voltage-dye images can show extra domains of similar membrane potential after a gap-junction blocker, with the pattern relaxing over weeks as the animal remodels. Counting isopotential regions from DiBAC fluorescence is coarse, so the ten-day increase and thirty-day return are plausible but not sharply measured.

The induced outlines were followed past the end of regeneration and reported to drift back toward the Girardia shape without a second injury. Continued morphological remodeling after the blastema has formed is consistent with other planarian proportion-adjustment results.

If Dugesia lies between Girardia and Schmidtea in the particular canonical-variate space they built, a gradual return to the Girardia shape will pass through a Dugesia-like region. That geometric path does not by itself show a biologically staged visit to each species' developmental program.

An agent model with a few migration and signalling rules can be tuned to draw four head outlines, so reproduction of the silhouettes is unsurprising. A fitted two-cell-type simulation does not quantitatively establish that gap-junction-regulated migration and signalling are what produced the living morphologies.

Landing on a few coherent, species-like heads rather than tumors or failed regeneration argues against a purely nonspecific toxic collapse. Discrete outcomes can also come from knocking a canalized system off its usual path, so the result is evidence of specificity more than of a positive instructive signal.

Hexanol is a poor gap-junction blocker compared with octanol, and a matched three-day exposure was reported not to change head shape. That control makes a generic long-chain-alcohol effect unlikely, though it does not prove octanol acted only on gap junctions.

Altering bioelectric connectivity can change regenerative anatomy without changing the genome, so physiological state is a real input to morphology. Calling that input previously unrecognized overstates the history of bioelectric patterning, and deriving other species' anatomies is a stronger claim than the shape shifts demonstrate.

Octanol itself is not expected to remain in planarian tissue for many days, and voltage patterns can still look abnormal after washout. Persistent change does not show that the cause is a rewired gap-junction network topology rather than longer-lived transcriptional or tissue damage.

A bath dose of octanol is unlikely to close every gap junction equally in every animal, and incomplete, variable block is consistent with several morphological outcomes. Variability of the voltage-dye effect does not by itself measure the fraction of junctions closed.

Failure of single voltage images to line up with head shape leaves room for a time-varying code, as in neural activity. It equally allows encoding in ion concentrations, gene expression, or junctional topology that a snapshot dye would miss, so the time-dependent account is not the most likely by default.

Planarians rebuild species-typical proportions after amputation, and these mis-specified heads kept changing toward the normal shape after large-scale regeneration had finished. That supports morphology as an actively maintained target, even though the claim does not identify the sensor that compares current shape with that target.

Differentiated planarian tissue influences neoblasts through positional signals, and gap-junction blockade changes regenerative outcomes, so some instructive cue may cross that interface. Secreted Wnt, BMP, and Hedgehog signals are the better-established guidance, and a specifically gap-junction-dependent somatic instruction is not shown.

Gap junctions are electrical synapses, so a network analogy between coupled somatic cells and neurons has a real biophysical basis. Nothing shows that planarian body cells obey the same statistical dynamics as brain circuits while they regenerate.

Discrete, mutually exclusive head shapes and a later return to the species-typical form fit an attractor picture in a loose sense. Identifying those states with other species' regions of evolutionary morphospace, and octanol as a kick into a neighboring species' attractor, is not established.

Temporary wrong heads that relax back over a few weeks can be described as local minima above a Girardia-shaped global minimum. Free energy was not measured, and amputation-as-raising-free-energy is a reinterpretation of injury and regeneration rather than a demonstrated physical quantity.

Planarian species share a core axial patterning system and differ by how its parameters are set, which makes some outcomes easier to reach than others. Evolutionary distance is not shown to be the same quantity as the ease of pushing that network into another species' head shape with a gap-junction blocker.

In Xenopus, hyperpolarizing a blastomere lineage distant from oncogene-expressing cells lowers the rate of induced tumor-like structures, so remote membrane voltage can influence whether those growths appear. Calling distant resting potential critical overstates a partial reduction in a tadpole assay that is not mammalian cancer.

Oncogene-driven masses in Xenopus tadpoles were reported to overproliferate, enlarge nuclei, become hypoxic and acidic, and attract leukocytes. Those are genuine overlaps with human tumor biology, while the structures remain induced tumor-like growths rather than full mammalian tumors.

Misexpressing a hyperpolarizing potassium channel away from the oncogene site was reported to cut Xrel3- and Gli1-induced masses by roughly a third, with sample sizes in the low hundreds. A similar reduction for two different oncogenes supports a voltage effect that is not oncogene-specific.

Elevated extracellular chloride, acting through native chloride conductances, was reported to reduce KRAS-driven tumor-like structures by a similar fraction to Kv1.5. That argues against a potassium-channel-specific artifact, with the caveat that a 70 mM chloride medium can affect embryos by more than membrane voltage.

Non-local wild-type CLIC1 strengthening chloride-linked suppression, and a dominant-negative CLIC1 blocking it, is the expected pattern if that channel carries the relevant chloride flux. Dominant-negative overexpression can have extra effects, so native CLIC1 is implicated rather than fully proven as the required mediator.

A dominant-negative HDAC1 placed away from the oncogene cells was reported to raise tumor-like incidence, which is evidence that histone deacetylase activity participates in the remote effect. One interfering construct does not establish HDAC1 as the main transduction step.

Antibiotic exposure can raise the incidence of these Xenopus growths, but the cocktail includes drugs that are not specific for gram-positive bacteria and that can stress embryonic cells directly. The jump from that increase to native butyrate-producing bacteria as the normal restraint on tumorigenesis is not secured.

Butyrate does inhibit histone deacetylases, so that biochemical link is real. The claim that resting-potential control of oncogene-driven growth in the tadpole is mediated by butyrate from native gram-positive bacteria is a chain of unconfirmed steps.

Tumor cells are often relatively depolarized, so some electrical signature exists in principle. A bidirectional long-range bioelectric message emitted by the tumor and readable at a distance is an untested speculation, not a shown property of tumor–host signalling.

Suppression by both potassium-channel and chloride-driven hyperpolarization points to membrane voltage, rather than one channel protein, as the operative variable in this assay. That supports a systems-level physiological cause in the Xenopus model without making resting potential a general master regulator of cancer.

The proposed sequence requires hyperpolarized membrane to present a lethal positive surface charge, to relocate butyrate-producing bacteria onto depolarized pre-neoplastic cells, and there to arrest the cell cycle via HDAC inhibition. Surface-charge microbiology and that spatial redistribution inside the embryo are not established.

Ion-channel drugs can change membrane potential and are already studied in cancer, so a therapeutic lead is conceivable if the remote-voltage effect is conserved. Conservation in mammalian tumors is unshown, and the prediction that approved channel drugs would yield new detection and treatment modalities is not yet borne out.

Nicotine is a known vertebrate teratogen, and exposure across neurulation at the stated dose was reported to raise major brain defects from a small control background to about half of tadpoles. The large incidence gap is a credible primary result of that experiment.

A bioelectric model with regionally different leak permeabilities and inward-rectifier potassium channels can produce a strongly hyperpolarized neural tube against depolarized flanks. Absolute values near −50 and −5 mV are model outputs that only roughly match what voltage dyes show in the neurula.

Nicotine was reported to flatten the neural-plate hyperpolarization by on the order of 15 mV, in the same direction the model predicted. Calibrated voltage-dye magnitudes in embryos are uncertain enough that the direction is more secure than the exact millivolt match.

Nicotine also acts on nicotinic receptors, but restoring the neural voltage pattern is sufficient to prevent the brain defects, which ties those defects to disruption of the prepattern. The bioelectric account explains the morphology result without ruling out parallel teratogenic pathways.

Brain patterning in this system is sensitive to the voltage difference between the neural midline and the lateral ectoderm, and depolarizing the neural domain is known to disturb it. That hyperpolarizing the lateral regions is similarly sufficient, and that the contrast acts by balancing proliferation, apoptosis, and gene expression, is less fully shown.

Inside their model, an HCN-like conductance that opens when already negative can be parameterized so that the neural tube runs away toward further hyperpolarization while depolarized flanks stay put. That positive feedback is a property of the chosen reversal potential, not the usual depolarizing effect of HCN current in neurons.

The model, with HCN2 opened preferentially in the already hyperpolarized neural tube, does predict that this pattern survives the nicotine-like perturbation. That is a statement about the simulation's output and matches the intervention they then tested.

Hcn2 RNA was reported to deepen neural hyperpolarization by about 15 mV, against a model prediction near 30 mV. A discrepancy of that size is a plausible and specifically reported limit of the model rather than a sign the measurement was invented.

In nicotine-treated neurulae, HCN2 expression was reported to bring back the neural-specific hyperpolarization that nicotine otherwise erases. Voltage-dye patterns support that restoration even if the absolute voltages are less certain than the spatial contrast.

A drop in minor brain-shape deviations from a small control background to a still smaller one is what the injections were reported to do. Percentages this low are sensitive to scoring thresholds, so the improvement beyond already healthy embryos is plausible but less firm than the nicotine rescue.

Hcn2 RNA was reported to bring nicotine-induced major brain defects from a majority of tadpoles down to the control background. That full morphological rescue is the central, quantitative result of the experiment and is backed by the non-conducting mutant control.

A pore mutant that does not conduct, injected on the same nicotine background, was reported to leave defect rates high. Dependence of the rescue on HCN2 conductance is the straightforward reading of that contrast.

Geometric morphometrics of stage-45 brains found a nicotine-associated shape shift relative to the head and no such shift when Hcn2 RNA was also injected. That agrees with the categorical scoring of rescued versus defective brains.

Nicotine-exposed tadpoles were reported to fail a light-avoidance learning assay that controls passed, with Hcn2 RNA restoring learning in most of a modest sample. An intact control rate of 100 percent is a brittle summary of a behavioral test, so the large rescue is more credible than the exact percentages.

Nicotine was reported to reduce or displace otx2 and xbf1, and Hcn2 RNA to return those forebrain and midbrain markers toward the normal pattern. In situ patterns are qualitative, but they connect the voltage rescue to the transcriptional sequence of brain regionalization.

A dominant-negative HCN2 that spares normal brain anatomy is evidence that native HCN2 is dispensable for ordinary patterning, and nicotine is not known to act by blocking that channel. A negative dominant-negative result can also mean the construct failed to inhibit, so the exclusion is reasonable rather than conclusive.

HCN2 both rescued nicotine and slightly cleaned up spontaneous defects, which suggests it can stabilize an endogenous voltage pattern. Extending that action to a wide range of teratogens and genetic lesions is an extrapolation from a single insult.

The model predicts that sharpening voltage-compartment boundaries should stabilize pattern, and HCN2 did so for the nicotine-sensitive brain prepattern. Confirmation for one context-sensitive channel does not show that reagents of this class generally reinforce developmental patterning.

Defining an agent by the events it can sense, model, and influence is a coherent functional proposal and makes dissimilar systems comparable. It is not, as a universal claim, the correct demarcation of every biological, artificial, and hypothetical self.

Many somatic cells still migrate, signal, and regulate, and tissues do pursue anatomical outcomes larger than one cell. Differentiated cells have also lost much of the behavioral range of free-living unicells, so the claim that those capacities were retained and merely rescaled is only partly right.

Regulative development and regeneration reach organ-scale anatomies that are not specified cell by cell: scrambled embryonic faces can still become normal faces, and structures such as kidney tubules hold a target geometry despite changed cell size. Those set points sit at the tissue and organ level.

When early left–right cues are disrupted, vertebrate embryos typically randomize as whole concordant individuals rather than as left–right mosaics, which is a domain-level decision. Body-wide melanocyte conversion in the tadpole model is a similar all-or-none tendency, though partial conversions also occur.

Ion channels and transmitters function in embryos long before neurons use them for movement, so a developmental origin of neural signalling is plausible. That motor control is specifically a sped-up exaptation of bioelectric navigation through anatomical morphospace is an evolutionary story, not a shown history.

The molecular hardware of excitability is ancient and shared between developing tissues and nervous systems, which supports deep homology of the mechanisms. Placing the cognitive capacities of advanced brains on a single continuum with those pre-neural processes is a contested inference from that conservation.

Loss of gap-junction coupling is associated with progression toward cancer, and restoring coupling or hyperpolarizing cells can suppress transformed behavior in the amphibian models. The further claim that the decisive variable is communication spread over long range, rather than cell-local damage, is only partly tested.

Depolarizing a selected cell population in otherwise genetically normal tadpoles can push melanocytes into a migratory, melanoma-like state, and hyperpolarization can block oncogene-induced tumor-like growth. Both effects are repeated findings in this amphibian system, not yet a general account of metastasis.

How far signals couple cells does change the spatial scale of coordinated behavior, and cancer often involves a breakdown of that coordination. Treating cancer cells, somatic cells, and unicells as equally selfish agents that differ only in the size of the self is a philosophical stipulation, not a result about selection.

Organisms are nested organizational levels, from molecular circuits to cells, organs, and groups. Calling each level a self whose persistence consists in restricting information from its neighbors is a theoretical overlay, and it is not true of most biological systems in that strong sense.

Goal-directed feedback is a useful criterion for agency and can mark which parts operate as one individual. Biological individuality is also fixed by genealogy, physiology, and evolutionary interests, so goal scale does not by itself determine the boundaries of an individual.

Nervous systems, larger bodies, and social organization have increased the spatial and temporal reach of what some lineages can sense and affect, and other lineages have simplified. A general expansion of cognitive boundaries through evolutionary time is a reasonable tendency, not a demonstrated law.

Developmental modules are explained by hierarchical gene regulation and cis-regulatory logic, and a single trigger can launch a cascade such as eye or limb formation. That modularity originated in memory and learning, with compression of experience into biophysical engrams, is not supported.

Some ion-channel families are shared between bacteria and animals, and membrane conductances are ancient sensors of the physical environment. Touch, taste, temperature, and hearing in animals are largely mediated by metazoan channel and receptor families, not by the same mechanisms bacteria used.
